newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japan's Yoshimura sees no significant surplus rise.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Yoshimura sees no significant surplus rise.

text.p: Yukio Yoshimura, the former deputy director general of Japan's Ministry of Finance International Finance Bureau, said on Thursday that Japan does not expect a significant rise in its trade surplus.

"The government is doing its best to stimulate the economy by strengthening domestic demand, so we will not see a significant increase in the surplus," Yoshimura told Reuters Financial Television in an interview on Thursday.
"This is the government's forecast and we still believe the forecast is the right one," he said.
Yoshimura was seconded from Japan's MOF on March 1 to take up the post of executive director for Japan at the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Japan's surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose sharply in January, marking the first increase in 17 months, the Finance Ministry announced on Thursday.
Yoshimura warned against making judgements on the long-term direction of Japan's trade acccount based on one month's data.
"We should not rely on one month's data to judge the situation. We would like to see the long-term development," Yoshimura said.
He said structural changes in Japan's economy which have encouraged Japanese companies to produce goods abroad should work to trim the surplus.
Asked about the long-term effect of a weakening yen on Japan's current account surplus, Yoshimura said that he does not see the change in the currency creating "an alarming situation."
"We do not see a significant problem right now," he said.
A weaker currency tends to improve a country's current account situation by making its exports relatively less expensive.
Yoshimura also said that Japan does not plan to bolster its economy through export growth.
"We have no intention of increasing exports to stimulate the economy. We will use domestic demand, not exports," he said.
